Coquette
koh-KET
noun / adjective (Gen-Z slang)
From French coquette, a flirt (feminine of coquet, a little rooster, a strutting man), in English since the 1600s for a woman who trifles with men’s affections. Revived on TikTok and Pinterest in 2023–2024 as the coquette aesthetic: pink, ribbons and bows, lace, pearls, ballet flats, a soft, girlish, hyper-feminine look. The online aesthetic drew openly on Lana Del Rey imagery and, in some corners, on the novel Lolita, a link many parents and critics flagged.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In current slang coquette names a style — bows in the hair, lace, pastel pink, pearls, a soft and girlish look. Many girls wear it innocently because it is pretty, and femininity is a good gift. The Christian observation: the old word still means what it meant, a woman who trades on allure, and the aesthetic’s roots are not innocent. Its online sources blend childlike dress with grown-up flirtation, and in places it borrows from a novel about the abuse of a girl. That combination — girlishness made alluring — is exactly what a father must refuse for his daughter. Scripture describes the coquette posture in Zion’s daughters, who "walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go" (Isa 3:16). And it guards the timing of romance: "stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please" (Son 8:4). Scripture’s femininity is not trifling but strong: the older women teach the younger "to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children" (Tit 2:4), and godly women are adorned "with good works" (1Ti 2:10). A father tells his daughter: bows and lace can be lovely; flirtation is not a game, girlhood is not a costume for anyone’s eyes, and "a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised" (Pro 31:30).

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen-Z slang (TikTok / Pinterest, 2023–2024) for a bows-and-lace hyperfeminine aesthetic, reviving an old word for a flirt — pretty in itself, troubling at its roots; Scripture guards girlhood and the timing of love.

COQUETTE, n. / adj. (Gen-Z slang, 2023–present; TikTok, Pinterest) A hyper-feminine aesthetic of bows, ribbons, lace, pearls, pastel pink, and ballet flats. "Her room is so coquette."

Often coquette aesthetic, coquette core.

Standard sense (since the 1600s): a woman who flirts to win admiration without serious intent.

Webster (1828), nearest root coquetry: “COQUETRY, noun Attempts to attract admiration, notice or love, from vanity; affectation of amorous advances; trifling in love.”

Decode for parents: often innocent taste in bows. Know the aesthetic’s sources, and keep girlhood from becoming a costume.

Key Scripture

Isa 3:16 — "Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet:"

Son 8:4 — "I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please."

Tit 2:4 — "That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children,"

1Ti 2:10 — "But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works."

Pro 31:30 — "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised."

Modern Corruption

Coquette revives a word for trifling allure and pairs girlish dress with flirtation; Scripture guards girlhood, forbids stirring up love before its time, and calls women to strong, sober femininity.

expand to see more

Femininity is a gift, and a girl who loves bows and lace is not doing anything wrong. The trouble is the package the trend arrived in. The word itself has always meant a woman who plays at love to win admiration; the online aesthetic mixed little-girl styling with adult allure, and some of its sources are frankly about a man’s abuse of a child. A culture that makes girlishness seductive is not honouring girls; it is exposing them.

Scripture guards both girlhood and love. "Stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please" (Son 8:4); the wanton eyes and mincing walk of Zion’s daughters drew the LORD’s rebuke (Isa 3:16). The femininity Paul commends is sober, loving, and adorned "with good works" (1Ti 2:10). Let your daughter wear the bow; teach her that her girlhood is not anyone’s aesthetic.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

French coq (rooster) → coquet, a strutting flirt → English coquette (1600s), a woman who trifles with affection → 2023–2024 TikTok "coquette aesthetic."
